The air in the family workshop was thick with the scent of sawdust and unspoken resentment. Liam stood before the easel, his hands stained with cerulean and ochre, while his father, Arthur, paced behind him, the rhythmic thud of his boots echoing like a countdown.

"Put the brush down, Liam," Arthur said, his voice low but vibrating with tension. "The contract for the new warehouse facade is on the table. It’s steady work. It’s *our* work."

Liam didn’t turn around. He could feel the weight of his father’s disappointment pressing against his back, heavier than any canvas. "It’s not just work, Dad. It’s a cage. I’ve been accepted into the city’s premier art residency. It’s a chance to actually *create* something that matters."

Arthur stopped pacing. The silence that followed was deafening. "Matter? You think your little paintings pay the bills? You think they keep this business alive? You’re throwing away three generations of hard work for a dream that won’t feed you."

"It’s not about feeding me!" Liam snapped, finally turning to face him. His heart hammered against his ribs. "It’s about who I am. I can’t breathe in this shop anymore. Every time I pick up a chisel, I feel like I’m betraying you. Every time I pick up a brush, I feel like I’m betraying myself."

Arthur’s face hardened, the lines around his eyes deepening. "Then you’re a fool. And when you’re hungry, don’t come crying back to this door. I won’t have a starving artist in my house."

Liam looked at the contract on the workbench, then at the vibrant, chaotic swirl of colors on his canvas. The rift between them wasn’t just a disagreement; it was a chasm. He realized then that choosing his art meant losing his father, and choosing his duty meant losing himself. The tension in the room was palpable, a live wire waiting to spark. He reached for his paintbrush, his hand trembling not from fear, but from the sheer, terrifying weight of the choice he was about to make.
